references.notes: “either a piece of the Epic of Gilgamesh or a fragment belonging with RS 22.421”

It might be thought that they are fragments of text from a Middle Babylonian version of Gilgameš that contained the Flood story, as told to the hero by Ūta-napišti—an antecedent of Tablet XI of the epic poem. Together with the Ark Tablet, they would then provide th evidence to show that already in the second millennium there was a version of the Gilgameš epic that contained the Flood story. However, it seems just as likely that a first-person account of the Flood circulated as an independent composition and was only later incorporated into the epic. The matter awaits more evidence.

variants.reconstruction:
%n ina pī (|) bibli || ina rēš (|) arhi
#note: On the reading @i{rēš arḫi}, see @bib{NABU1996-13}. According to @bib{wasserman2020flood@89}, the line reflects the tradition that the Flood started when the moon was invisible (on which see @bib{RN1780@209–210}), present in the Old Babylonian version (OB II 439b: @i{ana ūm warḫim}, “by the day of the New Moon”), in the SB version (SB III 92: @akk{[... u₂-b]i-il ar-hu} “[…] the month rea[ched its end],” and in MB Priv 50 (@akk{[... i-na u₄-mi-im] e#-ṭi#-i[m (x x x)]}, “[… on the] dimming [day]”). Unlike these traditions where the Flood starts on the new moon, Wasserman notes that this text presents the Flood as nearly finished on that date.
